source.title: On the effect of noise on fitting linear regression models

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double-descent risk curves using linear regression and noise-injection experiments rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own synthetic experiments, theoretical test-error results, scale comparison, and rice-data application. Cited findings from other work are not recorded. Numerical curve values are shown only in figures; the text describes the reported curve shapes and comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study measures test-error curves for OLS and minimum-norm OLS linear regression. It varies the number of predictors (adding noise predictors) and the number of observations (genuine, then zero-response noise observations), backed by closed-form and asymptotic risk results. This is a different method aimed at the same question on the size and sample axes, plus a real-data (rice SNP) sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find double descent both when adding noise predictors (overparameterized regime) and when adding noise observations (underparameterized regime), with apparently contradictory implications. They resolve this by arguing that noise-induced shrinkage, not model complexity, drives double descent. Equal null-model asymptotes plus the condition-number peak make double descent inevitable in their setup. They add that noise observations bias OLS and can make the optimal ridge parameter negative.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses OLS and minimum-norm OLS in linear-regression settings, adding irrelevant predictors or artificial noise observations; it does not reproduce deep-network or epoch-wise experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error minima depend on true dimension and signal-to-noise ratio; low signal-to-noise settings require more added noise observations to reach the lowest test error. Predictor scale affects the occurrence of multiple descents.

fits_no_version.finding: Noise predictors and zero-response noise observations shrink OLS/minimum-norm estimates toward zero, approximating ridge regression. Risk tends to the null-model risk at both ends of each axis, and with the condition-number peak this forces double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent is driven by implicit shrinkage from fitted noise and the interpolation condition-number blow-up, not by overparameterization itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Under many noise observations, the test-error-optimal ridge parameter can be negative, even with independent predictors in low dimension (Figure 6, Theorem 3.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit shrinkage from noise observations can over-regularize, making the optimal explicit ridge penalty negative.

record.code_released: Supplementary material states that a zipped folder contains R scripts for exact replication of the analyses and figures; no URL is stated.
record.problems: Most empirical curve values are presented only in figures, without numerical tables or reported uncertainty estimates. The sample-axis experiments append artificial observations with zero responses, so they do not establish the same result for additional genuine samples. The rice application uses 32 test accessions per split.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant own-result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Model classes other than linear regression (kernels, forests, networks).
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Direct manipulation of label noise, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak (Figure 6 reports only the sign of the optimal λ, not the resulting risk curve).

missing.what: Bias and variance components: both peak near interpolation, and variance falls to σ² in the overparameterized regime.
Heatmap of the optimal ridge λ, negative for large numbers of noise observations (d0=30, 500 trials).
Genuine-sample segment of the theoretical R(n): infinite risk at n∈{d0−1,d0} as true observations are added.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 untested-part statement is inaccurate. With n0≥d0, the n≈d0 peak is crossed with genuine observations, so V3 is tested for real samples in linear regression. Sample-axis rows were removed from V4 because V4 concerns capacity, not samples. Signal-to-noise variation in R1–R12 scales β rather than manipulating label noise, so it was not linked to V6. Theorem 3.1 is a cited prior result. All empirical values are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. Supplementary Figures S1 and S2 were not available in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The sample-size experiments append artificial noise observations with responses set to zero; the study does not test increasing the number of genuine observations from the data-generating distribution.
The study tests linear regression, not the full range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is defined and tested as predicting peak locations across size, epoch, and sample axes.

The study does not test whether optimally tuned regularization makes the double-descent peak disappear. It varies signal-to-noise settings and predictor scales, and studies noise predictors and noise observations rather than directly manipulating label noise.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.operation_detail: Theoretical test-error result for adding noise predictors.
rows.value: R(d) is infinite for d ∈ {n0 − 1, n0, n0 + 1}; as d → ∞ with d0 fixed, R(d) = σ² + ∥β0∥² + O(d⁻¹).
rows.note: The paper explains that the peak above the shared endpoint value entails a second descent in this setup.
rows.check: Drop V6. Theorem 3.1 is attributed to Breiman & Freedman and Belkin et al., so it is partly a cited result. The asymptote equals the null-model risk, so the second descent only returns to the null-model error.

relation.reason: The paper reports its own predictor-axis and observation-axis test-error results and analyses their interpolation peaks.

tranche.reason: OLS and minimum-norm linear regression provide empirical and theoretical tests of double descent using methods different from the deep-network experiments.

source_check.notes: Supplementary figures and algorithms are absent; R15–R16 are supported by explicit main-text statements only. The paper does not test deep-network, epoch-wise, effective-complexity or parameter-recounting claims, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.

statements.correction: Figures 1a and 1d: second descent present; underparameterized fit better. Theorem 3.3: R(d)→σ²+‖β0‖². These results support the local second-descent component of V4.
statements.problem: The empirical description is correct, but a better underparameterized optimum does not limit V4 as written: V4 requires improvement after interpolation, not a superior global optimum.
